newsitem.title: UK: Thousands remember N. Ireland's Bloody Sunday.
newsitem.headline: Thousands remember N. Ireland's Bloody Sunday.

text.p: Thousands of Catholics marched behind 14 white crosses on the 25th anniversary of "Bloody Sunday" to demand a fresh probe of the British army slaying of unarmed demonstrators that ignited the Northern Ireland conflict.

Martin McGuinness, chief strategist of the Irish Republican Army's political wing Sinn Fein, and a survivor of the 1972 civil rights march which came under army fire, said new evidence supported calls for an international investigation.

"I would like to support a call for an international public inquiry into the events of that day," he told a huge crowd which retraced the steps of the demonstration which came under fire from Britain's crack parachute regiment.

"On Bloody Sunday British troops came into this city, murdered 14 people and were decorated by the Queen and got away with it," said McGuinness, referring to honours bestowed on the regiment by the British monarch for overseas duty.

The march, one of the biggest staged in Northern Ireland's second city, climaxed a week of memorials and attempts by Irish nationalists and the Dublin government to get Britain to reopen one of the darkest chapters in Northern Ireland's history.
Thirteen Catholics taking part in a demonstration against internment without trial were killed when the paratroopers opened fire. A 14th died months later of his wounds.

An investigation by the then chief justice, Lord Widgery, heard army evidence that the troops believed they had come under fire during the demonstration, and returned it. He exonerated them of any blame.

McGuinness paid tribute to author Dun Mullan for a book published this month which says that evidence ignored by Widgery suggests that a sniper or snipers fired on the crowd from the walls of the city.

The Irish government, Britain's partner in a quest for a Northern Ireland settlement, is to collate the new evidence, which also includes intercepted army radio traffic and a study by an Irish law professor of unpublished army testimony.
It will then present it to the British government, which says that Bloody Sunday was a tragedy which does not warrant a fresh investigation until London gets new evidence.
Protestant Unionists, who want the province to stay British, say the tragedy is just one in the 27-year conflict.
They say the Irish Republican Army (IRA) is responsible for hundreds of deaths because of its continuing war against British rule of the province.

McGuinness said there would be no peace in Northern Ireland until a British leader arrived who had the stature of former South African leader F.W. de Klerk and invited Sinn Fein to all- party peace talks, as de Klerk did with Nelson Mandela.
Sinn Fein is barred from talks under way in Belfast on the province's future until the IRA calls a permanent and verifiable ceasefire.
It ended a 17-month truce 11 months ago, accusing Britain of delaying Sinn Fein's entry to the talks with impossible preconditions.

"Most of all we need a de Klerk type figure to walk out of the doors of 10 Downing Street (the British prime minister's offical residence)", McGuinness told a crowd that organisers estimated at up to 50,000. Reporters said it was up to 20,000-strong.
He called on British Prime Minister John Major to hold a general election before a May deadline to return a strong government which would tackle the Northern Ireland conflict.
He argued that Sinn Fein had created a brief honeymoon of peace in Northern Ireland through the IRA's 17-month truce which could still be revived.
"The next British government needs to understand that there is still the hope and the opportunity which we helped to create," he said.
Britain says the IRA truce was a tactical ploy and that the guerrillas were never prepared to give up violence in pursuit of their goal of a united Ireland.
